She brought suit against the city in federal court, arguing that her business was taken without just compensation under the Fifth Amendment Takings Clause and that she was denied procedural due process under the Fourteenth Amendment. The court granted a motion to dismiss because she did not possess a property interest that was implicated, including in the license and permits. She appealed. Will the federal Court of Appeals affirm the trial court’s dismissal of her case?
A. Yes, because there is no right to earning a living under the substantive due process clause.
B. Yes, because the state interest in protecting the public from illegal activities required the state action that was taken.
C. No, because once the parlor had opened with all the proper permits, it could not be deprived of its licenses for any reason until they were up for renewal.
D. No, because she had a property right in her license and permits, which were taken without any procedural due process.

options.A: Yes, because there is no right to earning a living under the substantive due process clause.
options.B: Yes, because the state interest in protecting the public from illegal activities required the state action that was taken.
options.C: No, because once the parlor had opened with all the proper permits, it could not be deprived of its licenses for any reason until they were up for renewal.
options.D: No, because she had a property right in her license and permits, which were taken without any procedural due process.
